sections.h2: Why does Bulloch County, Georgia, work differently from its neighbors?
sections.html:
Bulloch County is a university county in southeast Georgia. Statesboro is the seat, and Georgia Southern University and East Georgia State College's Statesboro campus are both there, with Ogeechee Technical College in an unincorporated part of the county (Wikipedia). The county was created on February 8, 1796, spans roughly 673 square miles and is mostly flat coastal plain.

The 2020 count was 81,099 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 86,949. Half the county's occupied homes, 50.1 percent, were rented in 2020, and the median resident was 28.9 years old. Census QuickFacts adds a median home value of $222,500 for 2020 to 2024, owner occupancy of 53.1 percent and 1,389 building permits in 2025.

The result is a county of student rentals, investor houses and family homes. Many sellers hold a rental or an inherited house, and the tax questions below apply to both.

sections.h2: Where does Bulloch County property tax get handled?
sections.html:
The county's government offices keep weekday hours of 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., according to the county website. Bulloch splits the work in a way that differs from most Georgia counties. The tax assessors, not the tax commissioner, receive tax returns and homestead applications.

Bulloch County property tax contacts, from the county's assessor, tax commissioner and payment pages

The commissioner lists propertytax@bullochcounty.net for tax questions. The county's online tax record search and payment portal are linked from the tax commissioner page. Card payments carry a convenience fee charged by the processor, not by the county.

For a quick answer on whether a bill is current, the online tax record search is faster than calling. Use the office phones for payoff letters and for anything that involves an exemption or a correction to the record.

sections.h2: How does Bulloch County value property and take returns?
sections.html:
Fair market value is set as of January 1, and the tax is levied on an assessed value that is 40 percent of it. One mill equals one dollar for each thousand dollars of assessed value. The county commissioners set the county rate, and the school board sets its own, as the assessors' page explains.

Every owner must file an initial return covering real and personal property held on January 1. Bulloch takes returns from January 1 through April 1 at the assessors' office. That first return then carries forward at the last finalized value, and a new one is needed only after you add property, make improvements or want to declare another value.

Email returns are refused. A faxed return has to be in the office by 5:00 p.m. on the closing day of the appeal period, and the board has no power to waive penalties or stretch a deadline.

Millage rate hearings took place in August 2026, and the county home page carries the presentation.

sections.h2: How does an appeal work in Bulloch County?
sections.html:
An appeal must be written and filed within 45 days after the date of the notice of change. Email appeals are turned away, and a fax must land by 5:00 p.m. on the last day.

The path runs through four steps:

  • First you file with the Board of Tax Assessors, which reviews the appeal and answers you.
  • When the board leaves the value alone, the case moves to the County Board of Equalization for a hearing.
  • At filing, you can pick arbitration over that hearing.
  • Anyone still dissatisfied can take the matter to Superior Court.

Grounds are taxability, value or how uniform the value is against similar properties. A complaint about the tax amount does not qualify, because that follows the millage rate. The county's How Do I page also has a request link for property tax assessment appeals.

sections.h2: Which Bulloch County exemptions can lower the bill?
sections.html:
The assessors describe several homestead exemptions. Each requires that you own the home and live in it as your legal residence on January 1, and applications run from January 1 to April 1. A granted exemption renews yearly until ownership changes.

  • Standard homestead: a $2,000 deduction from the 40 percent assessed value.
  • Age 65 and up: $4,000 off state and county taxes for households inside the income cap the page lists.
  • Age 62 and up: a school tax exemption capped at $10,000 of assessed value, with its own income cap.
  • Disabled veterans and surviving spouses of military members: bigger exemptions under state law.

A deferral program also exists for homeowners 62 and older who pass an income test. Deferred tax generally comes due when ownership changes or the balance reaches 85 percent of the property's value, so a sale ends the deferral.

Farm owners may apply by April 1 for a conservation use covenant. It runs ten years, costs a $10 recording fee and carries a penalty of twice the taxes saved if broken, so talk to the assessors before selling covenanted land.

sections.h2: How do rentals, schools and highways affect a Bulloch County sale?
sections.html:
Bulloch had 32,983 housing units in 2020, and 9.8 percent sat empty. Rentals stood vacant at a 9.0 percent rate against 1.4 percent for owner homes. Median gross rent for 2020 to 2024 is $995, and a mortgaged owner pays a median $1,462 a month. A landlord selling a Statesboro rental is courting buyers in a county where about half of occupied homes were rented in 2020.

Public schooling comes from one countywide district, Bulloch County School District, plus a charter school, Statesboro STEAM Academy, chartered through another district. Families ask about school zones, and commuters ask about I-16, US 301, US 80 and US 25, all of which cross the county.

  • Student rentals near the university are priced and bought differently than family homes.
  • Rural tracts outside Statesboro often carry farm or timber use, so ask the assessors about covenants first.
  • The county has a separate timber harvest page, worth checking if trees were cut before the sale.

Pull the online tax record for any parcel before listing. It shows what the assessors have on file, which makes a wrong acreage or missing exemption easy to spot.

sections.h2: Does a Bulloch County city send its own tax bill?
sections.html:
Four of them do. Statesboro, Brooklet, Portal and Register each bill and collect real and personal property tax on their own, so a house inside their limits draws one bill from the county and a second from the city.

That matters at closing. Your payoff request should cover both bills, and the title company has to know which city, if any, holds your parcel.

At sale time, get a payoff from the commissioner and ask the person handling your closing how this year's share will be divided; the due date appears on the bill. Landlords should also check that the owner name on each bill matches the deed before closing.

faqs.q: Which office takes homestead applications in Bulloch County?
faqs.a: The Tax Assessors, at 113 North Main Street in Statesboro. They accept applications from January 1 through April 1, and a granted exemption renews on its own.

faqs.q: What is the appeal window in Bulloch County?
faqs.a: The window is 45 days after the notice date. File in writing, since the assessors do not take appeals by email.

faqs.q: Does a Statesboro homeowner receive one tax bill or two?
faqs.a: Two. Statesboro collects its own real and personal property tax, so the county sends one bill and the city sends another every year.

faqs.q: How do I pay Bulloch County property tax?
faqs.a: Pay the Tax Commissioner in person at Suite 101, 113 North Main Street, Statesboro, or online through the county's payment link. Questions go to 912-764-6285. Cards add a convenience fee from the processor.

faqs.q: Can the Bulloch assessors forgive a late filing penalty?
faqs.a: No. The assessors say they lack authority to relieve penalties or grant filing extensions, so meet each stated deadline.
